Rain Begins to Pour Down in Bandung, Rainy Season Not Yet Arrived 
 CUACA Rain Begins to Pour Down in Bandung, Rainy Season Not Yet Arrived
 Rain has begun to fall frequently in Bandung, but the Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) says the rainy season hasn't arrived yet. Residents are urged to be alert for potential hydrometeorological disasters.
 26 Okt 2026 15:23 WIB · Lingkungan 
 RONY ARIYANTO NUGROHO
 Kecil Sedang Besar Sangat Besar Share
 Copy Link
 By Cornelius Helmy Herlambang, Fabio Maria Lopes Costa 
 This article has been translated using AI. See original . 
 00:00 00:00 10 10 1.00x Rain has been pouring down on Bandung and its surrounding areas for the past three days. Residents are wondering if the rainy season has arrived.
 After a long dry spell, Husein, a resident of Padasuka in Bandung, West Java, forgot to store his raincoat in the seat of his motorcycle. As a result, when heavy rain suddenly poured down on Saturday (24/10/2026) afternoon, he was forced to take shelter in front of a closed shop window.
 "Is it actually the rainy season yet? They say it's November, but it's still October and it's already raining," he said.
 Nunung, a cracker maker in Cimenyan, Bandung Regency, was also overwhelmed. Rain disrupted her small-scale cracker production.
 "For the past four days, the sun hasn't shone as brightly as usual. It's good for me because I don't feel overheated. But it's not great for drying the crackers. There has been more cloud cover and rain," said Nunung.
 So, has the rainy season really arrived?
 Patria Wirayudha, a forecaster at the West Java Climatology Station, stated that rain has indeed fallen in Bandung and its surrounding areas in recent times. The rainfall intensity recorded over the last ten days has reached 55 millimeters.
 However, according to Patria, this condition cannot yet be concluded as the start of the rainy season. The current phenomenon still represents a transitional period from the dry season to the rainy season.
 "It's called the rainy season when the intensity reaches 150 millimeters in three decades or for 30 days," he said.
 Patria explained that the rainfall in Bandung and its surrounding areas is largely influenced by local factors. One of these is the region's proximity to mountains, which facilitates the development of rain clouds.
 "It is expected that the rainy season will begin in West Java generally during the second and third decades of November. Currently, there is still localized rainfall in certain areas," said Patria.
 He added that rain during the transitional period can occur suddenly, with intensity ranging from heavy to extreme. Rain can also last for hours and may recur over several days.
 "The potential for heavy to extreme rainfall during the transitional period is very high. The public is urged to enhance their vigilance and mitigation efforts against hydrometeorological disasters," he advised.
 Regarding this condition, disaster expert Surono has repeatedly warned of the potential dangers following a long dry season.
 According to Surono, the prolonged drought resulting from the El Niño phenomenon can lead to the formation of numerous cracks in the ground in several areas. When rainwater seeps into these cracks, the potential for significant landslides increases.
 "The weight of the water-saturated soil becomes extremely heavy, compromising the stability of the area. If a landslide occurs, it can happen on a large scale," he said.
 This situation needs to be addressed proactively. To date, many Indonesians, including those in West Java, continue to reside in disaster-prone areas, such as on cliffs, near springs, and along rivers susceptible to flash floods.
 "The city and district governments can map out potential natural disaster risks early on using vulnerability maps provided by the Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation at the Geological Agency. These maps can serve as a tool to reduce disaster risks, including collaborating with the community to seal any ground fissures that appear and pose a landslide threat," he said.
 Hadi Rahmat Hardjasasmita, a junior public relations officer at the West Java Regional Disaster Management Agency (BPBD), stated that natural disasters remain a potential threat during the transition from the dry season to the rainy season.
 "All personnel from the BPBD across 27 regencies and cities in West Java have been put on alert in disaster-prone areas," said Hadi.
 West Java is one of the provinces highly vulnerable to hydrometeorological disasters. In 2025, data from the West Java Disaster Mitigation Agency (BPBD) recorded approximately 1,500 disaster incidents, resulting in 79 fatalities and affecting 750,266 residents.
 "We urge residents living near riverbanks and mountain slopes to seek safe shelter if heavy rain lasts for more than an hour," he said.
